items.prose: A sentiment vendor's backtest covers 2,520 trading days. Its scoring model's training cut-off falls after day 2,016, and the vendor says 25 prompt and model versions were tried before the one it sells.

parts.question: What share of the backtest lies after the cut-off? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the days after day 2,016.

byKey.before: 0.8 is the share before the cut-off.

parts.question: Using the 504 clean days from part 1, how many years of 252 trading days is the clean window? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the clean days by 252.

parts.question: Over those 2 clean years, what Sharpe ratio does the best of 25 noise strategies reach, by $\sqrt{2\ln N}/\sqrt T$? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.one-year: You left out $\sqrt T$: with $T = 2$, divide by $\sqrt 2$.

parts.question: The vendor's clean-window Sharpe ratio is 2.4. Taking 1.7941 from part 3 as the noise best, what is the haircut Sharpe ratio? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Subtract part 3's figure from 2.4.

explain.text: $2.4 - 1.7941 = 0.6059$: most of the reported figure is what 25 tries of noise could reach.

parts.question: Over 2 years, a Sharpe ratio needs about $1.96/\sqrt 2 = 1.39$ to clear 1.96 standard errors. Is the haircut figure from part 4 clear of noise?

options.why: Positive is not the bar; it must clear about 1.39.

options.text: Yes: the raw 2.4 clears the bar
options.why: The raw figure is the best of 25; the haircut one is what counts.

feedback.correct: No: the haircut Sharpe ratio is far below the bar for two years.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare part 4's figure with the bar.

explain.text: 0.6059 against a bar of 1.39: the vendor has not shown a signal, only a selected backtest.

items.prose: A desk builds a news feature for a 16:30 close. On Tuesday two notes arrive, at 09:10 (score 0.6) and 16:40 (score −0.4); on Wednesday one, at 12:00 (score 0.3).

parts.question: How many of the three notes can Tuesday's close use?

feedback.correct: One: the 16:40 note arrived after the close.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare each time with Tuesday 16:30.

byKey.by-date: Two counts the 16:40 note, which came after the close.

explain.text: Only the 09:10 note was out by Tuesday 16:30, so 1 note feeds that close.

parts.question: Using the timing from part 1, what is Wednesday's mean score over the notes published since Tuesday's close? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Include the note that missed Tuesday's close.

byKey.wed-only: You dropped the 16:40 note; it feeds Wednesday.
byKey.sign: Check the sign: the late note's −0.4 outweighs Wednesday's 0.3.

explain.text: The late Tuesday note and Wednesday's note give a mean of −0.05.

parts.question: With a half-life of 1 day, what weight does the 09:10 Tuesday note get at Wednesday's close? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Measure the age from 09:10 Tuesday to 16:30 Wednesday in days.

byKey.one-day: The note is more than a day old: 31 hours and 20 minutes.

explain.text: 31 hours 20 minutes is 1.3056 days, so the weight is 0.4046.

items.prose: A quant tests whether a model's sentiment scores depend on company names. Six headlines are scored raw and with the names masked; the changes, raw minus masked, are 0.22, −0.02, 0.02, 0.22, −0.01 and 0.19.

parts.question: What is the mean change? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the six changes.

byKey.sum: That is the sum; divide by 6.

explain.text: The changes sum to 0.62, so the mean is 0.1033.

parts.question: Their standard deviation is 0.1181. Using the mean from part 1, what is its standard error? Give 4 decimal places.

byKey.sd: That is the standard deviation itself.

parts.question: With mean 0.1033 and standard error 0.0482, how many standard errors from 0 is the mean change? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the mean by its standard error.

byKey.inv: You divided the standard error by the mean.

explain.text: 2.14 standard errors: suggestive, on only six headlines.

parts.question: Using the 2.14 standard errors from part 3, what should the quant do next?

options.text: Mask many more headlines before concluding
Declare the model leaky and drop it
options.why: About two standard errors on six headlines is not proof.

options.text: Declare the model clean of names
options.why: A mean change of about 0.1 is not small; the sample is.

options.text: Stop, since masking tests do not work
options.why: They work; six headlines is too few.

feedback.correct: More headlines: the evidence is suggestive, not conclusive.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Is six headlines enough?

explain.text: Three of the six headlines dropped by about 0.2 when masked; a few hundred headlines would settle whether names drive the scores.
